Issued at 250 PM EDT Fri Oct 16 2026

Rest of Today-Tonight...High moisture in light SE-E flow under 
weak high pressure is supporting isolated to widely scattered 
showers and lightning storms on the inland moving sea breeze. 
Modest SW-S flow in the mid-levels is producing some training of 
heavy rainfall, as well as slow to nearly stationary movement of 
individual cells, which could result in locally high rainfall 
amounts of 2-4". Due to a combination of saturated soils and 
potential for heavy rainfall, most of East Central Florida remains
outlook in a Marginal (level 1 of 4) risk for excessive rainfall 
leading to flash flooding. Only portions of Lake and Volusia 
counties to the north aren't included. Soundings show a typical 
late wet season profile, with a nearly saturated atmosphere, warm
mid-levels, and modest instability. A couple storms that managed 
to find a more favorable environment have been observed early this
afternoon, producing occasional lightning strikes, and other 
storms that manage to develop the rest of the afternoon and
evening may produce more frequent lightning and wind gusts up to 
45 mph. Activity will trend inland with the Atlantic breeze, 
colliding with the Gulf breeze over the interior in the evening. 
This activity is forecast to wander back towards the east coast 
through the early overnight, generally dissipating or moving 
offshore after midnight. Mostly dry conditions through the rest of
the night until the next front arrives Saturday morning.

Temperatures will be above normal, ranging from the upper 80s 
along the coast to upper 80s/low 90s inland. More humid conditions
today will also produce peak heat index values around 98-102F. 
Warm and muggy conditions continue overnight, with lows in the low
to mid 70s. 

Saturday-Thursday...Prolonged breezy to windy northeasterly flow 
will produce hazardous beach and marine conditions through much of
the coming week. The pressure gradient tightens across the 
Florida peninsula Saturday between a cold front pushing through 
the area, high pressure building into the eastern US behind the 
front, and a disturbance developing on the front near the Atlantic
seaboard. The front stalls over South Florida to the Straits of 
Florida Sunday, as the low pressure system becomes cut off over 
the western Atlantic waters off the eastern seaboard seaboard, and
the high settles north and west of the front/low. These three 
features are forecast to move very little through at least the 
first half of next week, keeping the pressure gradient tight and 
continuing strong northeasterly flow. The greatest uncertainty in 
the forecast lies with position and strength of the developing 
low, which models are still waffling on, and has resulted in 
forecast winds coming down a little from the previous package. 
However, this is just one model cycle, and NBM probabilities for 
gusts approaching Wind Advisory criteria along the coast remain 
moderate to high (40-70%) late Saturday into Sunday. Therefore 
will continue to message sustained wind speeds could reach 15-20 
mph inland, up to 20-25 mph along the coast, with gusts 30-35 mph 
possible across much of the area the next several days. Gusts 
could push to 40 mph along the coastal corridor late Saturday 
through Sunday, and into Monday. The pressure gradient is forecast
to loosen a little going toward mid-next week as the high weakens
and the low drifts north, allowing winds to ease a bit, but 
conditions are forecast to remain breeze to windy. This extended 
period of fresh onshore flow will produce rough surf, large 
breaking waves, and a high risk of life-threatening rip currents.
Entering this dangerous water is highly discouraged! Long period 
onshore swells will also likely contribute to moderate beach 
erosion through multiple high tide cycles. High Surf Advisories, 
Rip Current Statements, and Coastal Flood Advisories will likely 
be needed in upcoming forecast packages.

As for rain chances, the prospect for lightning storms along and 
ahead of the front Saturday morning for the northern counties is 
decreasing, but can't be completely ruled out. Best chances remain
in the southern counties (Treasure Coast to Okeechobee) where 
daytime heating will be able to destabilize before the front 
arrives. Overall rain chances Saturday reflect the storm chances, 
lower (20-40%) across the north, and higher (50-80%) across the 
south. Models have consistently signaled potential for multiple 
rounds of heavy showers and storms late Saturday into the 
overnight across the southernmost counties, mainly Martin, that 
could produce locally high rainfall amounts 2-4" leading to 
flooding, and 1 in 10 chance of amounts in excess of 6" producing 
flash flooding in one or two places, especially given how 
saturated soils are. There is a Slight (level 2 of 4) for 
excessive rainfall for coastal Martin into southern portions of 
coastal St. Lucie counties. Other convective hazards will include
